newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Donors say Ivorian coffee revival plan not needed.
newsitem.headline: Donors say Ivorian coffee revival plan not needed.

text.p: Ivory Coast, flush with coffee, should scrap its five-year Coffee Rehabilitation Plan as the scheme's 300,000-tonnes objective looks set to be reached in 1996/97 (Oct-Sept), donor sources said on Thursday.
"It hasn't really started but the plan is already irrelevant," said one source close to June talks between donors and Ivorian officials on commodity reforms under a 1995 $150 million World Bank loan.

"Ivory Coast has already accepted the 300,000 tonnes as the figure for this year," he added, referring to industry estimates of a 1996/97 coffee crop already well above 1995/96's 180,000 tonnes with three months of the season to go.

Ivory Coast set a higher than usual farmgate price of 695 CFA a kilo for 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) and even though world prices went into a late 1996 tailspin farmers had by then given trees more attention, according to crop analysts.

It forecast 230,000 tonnes for 1996/97 from 180,000 tonnes the year before and cut farmgate prices to 495 CFA a kilo, balanced by an export tax cut to 10 CFA from 150 CFA, which donors see unchanged in 1997/98.
Arrivals of coffee at ports totalled around 290,000 tonnes by mid-June, port sources said.
"The (partly European Union-funded rehabilitation plan) funds have already been disbursed but not much spent," said the donor source.
Under the plan, funding had been earmarked for replanting stock, educating farmers and rehabilitating coffee trees neglected after a late 1980s coffee price meltdown.

Like many other African countries, Ivory Coast has an ageing tree stock, with some nearly 40 years old, but maintenance and a peak in the poor-moderate-strong yield cycle had helped boost yields -- despite bean quality problems from sloppy husbandry.
Donors and industry sources disagree on the best way to avoid a repeat of recent poor quality produce discounts at ports.

The World Bank wants complete liberalisation of internal and external marketing prices and says an annual list of "reference" farmgate and marketing chain prices (baremes) set by Ivory Coast should be abolished.
"No more talks of a bareme, no more talk of a minimum price," one source told Reuters. "We hope there will be no bareme for 1997/98," -- for coffee or cocoa.
Marketing prices were fixed by the Caistab marketing board until 1995/96 but donors say the "reference" tariff cuts out price-bargaining.

"Farmers should be at the centre of economic decision making and be rewarded for being good," he said. "Quality is already down. It has nothing to do with closing upcountry quality centres (in 1995/96). It is because prices are still fixed and provide no incentive for effort," he said.
Grading of poorly sorted and badly stored coffee has taken up exporters' time and resulted in costs being passed back down the chain, he added. Exports had been slowed by grading times.

Some donors see internal marketing liberalisation as responsible for drops in coffee as well as cocoa quality. Coffee reforms are being watched closely as they should serve as a test-bed for more cocoa sector liberalisation expected in 1999/2000 at the earliest.
